Switchable altermagnetism and Luttinger-compensated ferrimagnetism in graphene-MnPS3 heterostructures
Error-controlled switching between discrete and continuum dislocations in a unified defect framework
abstract: Simulating defects of every dimension together is expensive, and the savings of adaptive methods are rarely tested at equal accuracy. We present a variational framework in which fields, dislocation lines and defect densities share one free energy, one dissipation law and exact ledgers of mass and Burgers vector, so that a region can change its representation without gaining or losing defects. On this basis, an allocator switches the dislocations themselves between discrete particles, where they are sparse, and a continuous density, where they are dense. The switch is made block by block from local counts, conserves the Burgers vector exactly and is controlled by a single threshold. For $5\times10^5$ dislocations, the allocator reproduces the discrete model to within 1% in the sparse region at 14-37 times lower cost, depending on the machine; the advantage grows to 81 times at $10^6$ dislocations, and a threshold calibrated on one ensemble meets its error target on an independent one. For an idealized array of dislocation walls in copper, the allocator is 37.5 times cheaper than particle dislocation dynamics and, at almost the same cost, six times more accurate than continuum dislocation dynamics between the walls. In a three-dimensional copper model coupling grain-boundary cavitation with damage, ligaments left at nominal coalescence delay creep rupture by 25-48% (post hoc sweep). By contrast, grids refined at interfaces gain less than twofold once the active region exceeds about 30% of the domain, so representation switching, rather than grid refinement, is the effective form of adaptivity for defect-rich microstructures.

title: Nonadiabatic polaron dynamics from machine-learned hopping trajectories
abstract: The formation and motion of small polarons are ubiquitous in energy materials and influence photoinduced processes. Polaron transport is governed by thermally activated lattice dynamics and rare hopping events, requiring spatial and temporal scales only attainable with machine-learning molecular dynamics, which enables extensive sampling of atomic trajectories and polaron configurations over nanoseconds. Moreover, the Born-Oppenheimer approximation underlying standard ab initio molecular dynamics cannot describe the nonadiabatic coupling between electronic states mediated by nuclear motion, which controls energy exchange and excited-state relaxation. Here, we develop a simulation framework that combines machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics with nonadiabatic molecular dynamics to bridge these complementary aspects of polaron physics, and determine how different polaron-hopping mechanisms affect excited-state dynamics. The enlarged trajectory space allows us to provide the first direct dynamical confirmation of the adiabatic or nonadiabatic classification of polaron hopping regimes originally proposed on the basis of static Marcus-theory arguments, and to connect individual hopping events directly to nonadiabatic electronic transitions. In bulk TiO$_2$, nonadiabatic hoppings occur preferentially when the energy of the polaron-induced gap state approaches the conduction-band manifold, promoting both electronic de-excitation and, via a Landau-Zener mechanism, excitation from the ground state. In MgO, the predominantly adiabatic character of hole-polaron hopping suppresses these effects, leading to longer charge-carrier lifetimes and an absence of thermally activated excitations. At the rutile TiO$_2$(110) surface, hopping events are rarer than in bulk because the excess electron is strongly stabilized in the subsurface region, leading to correspondingly longer de-excitation times.

title: A practical route to amorphous solid-state electrolyte structures by hybrid reverse Monte Carlo with foundation potentials
abstract: Amorphous alkali oxychlorides are fast ion conductors, but their atomic structure remains unresolved. Total scattering sums all partial pair correlations into one curve that has no unique inversion, so the structure must be modeled. Melt-quench molecular dynamics builds a model from the interatomic potential alone, and reverse Monte Carlo (RMC) builds one from the measurement alone. The two have rarely been compared with all else held fixed. We benchmark both routes and two hybrid schemes on amorphous \ce{Li_{0.9}NbO_{0.9}Cl_{4.1}} against one neutron pair distribution function with one foundation potential. The hybrid schemes put the energy either in the acceptance rule (inline) or in short relaxations between blocks of refinement (alternating). Each refinement starts from a melt-quench glass or from a random packing of isolated units. The glass has the lowest energy and places the first-shell peaks correctly, but carries almost none of the oscillation beyond 6~Å (goodness of fit $R^{2} = 0.29$). Pure RMC fits the measurement to within its counting noise ($R^{2} = 0.99$), but at more than $1.3$~eV/atom above the glass, and niobium loses about half of its first-shell chlorine. Started from the glass, both hybrid schemes reach $R^{2} = 0.92$ within $0.1$~eV/atom of its energy and keep its coordination chemistry. Structures from the two inputs fit almost equally well and differ in energy by a tenth of the RMC penalty, yet they differ in whether their polyhedra are connected. The input is therefore part of the method. We recommend quenching a glass with a foundation potential and refining it against the measurement with a hybrid scheme. The resulting structure carries both the local chemistry and the medium-range order, and it is the starting point for modeling ion transport in these conductors.

title: Text-Informed Training Data Filtering for Enhanced Virtual Flow Meter Performance
abstract: In sectors such as energy, aquaculture and chemical processing, the effectiveness of both mechanistic and data-driven models is frequently limited by poor-quality training data, which obscures underlying physical laws and degrades predictive accuracy. Such quality issues commonly manifest as anomalies in the dataset, ranging from sensor faults to process upsets and incorrect operator inputs. While traditional rule-based filtering can remove a subset of the anomalies, it is unable to leverage contextual information stored as unstructured text, such as engineer comments and operational logs that explain under what conditions the data was collected. We propose a text-informed data filtering method that leverages large language models (LLMs) to integrate unstructured operational data with tabular sensor data. The method consists of two steps: (1) contextual anomaly detection by reasoning over both data modalities, and (2) generation of a binary mask that is applied to filter the training dataset for model development. To investigate the potential benefit, a steady-state soft-sensor regression model, namely a virtual flow meter that estimates well flow rates, is used as the downstream evaluation target. Experiments on a synthetic oil and gas dataset show improved model performance compared to traditional rule-based filtering. Ablation studies show that textual operator comments can provide filtering-relevant signals beyond sensor data alone, with the multimodal approach reducing downstream MAPE from 7.1% to 5.4% relative to sensor-only filtering. This work demonstrates that integrating unstructured operational knowledge with sensor data through LLMs can improve data quality for industrial machine learning applications, offering a scalable alternative to manual data curation.

title: One Monitor Does Not Fit All: Formalism-Agnostic Runtime Verification for Agentic AI
abstract: Agentic AI systems combine model decisions, mutable state, tool calls, and delegation to external agents. Monitoring them requires observations from different execution boundaries, while prevention requires control before an operation produces its effect. We present AgenticRV, a runtime-verification architecture that separates these boundaries from the monitoring formalism. Adapters emit canonical events; each monitor receives its own projection and abstraction; and a decision policy uses normalised verdicts to select a reaction supported by the responsible adapter. We formalise when observations suffice, monitor replacement preserves decisions, and blocking prevents unsafe effects. We also distinguish rejected attempts from completed effects, avoiding the assumption that a blocked request must leave every monitor in a permanent violation state. The Python implementation supports LangGraph, MCP, and A2A. A controlled LangGraph experiment combines an external Reelay temporal monitor with a programmatic report monitor; ablations show why both are needed for the selected requirements. Differential checks and cross-adapter tests provide further integration evidence. An LLM-driven incident-response example illustrates the same enforcement path, while existing microbenchmarks isolate framework costs. The results support reuse of monitoring methods at explicit control boundaries, subject to the stated observation and deployment assumptions.

title: ReproBAIT: Can coding agents build their own biological AI tools?
abstract: Large language models are increasingly competent at leveraging scientific knowledge and existing computational tools to execute complex workflows. At present, little information exists on their ability to reconstruct tools when given limited descriptions of such tools. We introduce an evaluation titled ReproBAIT (Reproducing Biological AI Tools), which measures the ability of coding agents to design, implement, and train biological AI tools taken from published research across a range of information access conditions. The coding agent is securely sandboxed without internet access and receives training data, a fixed time and compute budget, and limited information about the tool to replicate. We then score the reproduced biological AI tool based on its performance (tool-specific metrics) on held-out data. We evaluated a set of biological AI tools of varying complexities: ProteinMPNN, an inverse protein folding tool, RFdiffusion3, an all-atom generative diffusion tool, and a closed-source molecular design tool. We institute a methodology to check for memorisation, as the open source tools are likely to be included in models' pretraining corpus. Across a range of leading closed- and open-source coding agents, we find substantial reproduction capability for some selected tools, though limited capability for a highly complex tool. We find moderate evidence consistent with memorisation, varying across coding agents. These results suggest that tool developers need to be increasingly cautious when releasing information about the tools publicly; re-creation of the tool based on such information could undermine a tool's commercial value or invalidate dual-use managed access strategies.

title: Magnetic field induced modulation of heat transport in CrPS$_4$ probed by TaIrTe$_4$ transverse Seebeck thermometry
abstract: Understanding and controlling heat flow in low-dimensional magnetic materials is central to thermoelectrics and spin caloritronics. One of the challenges is the absence of sensitive probes of small, field-dependent modulations in thermal transport. Here we demonstrate transverse Seebeck thermometry using exfoliated TaIrTe$_4$ as a probe of thermal conductivity modulated by an external magnetic field on a van der Waals magnet, CrPS$_4$. With a temperature gradient oriented at $45^\circ$ to its principal crystallographic axes, TaIrTe$_4$ exhibits a transverse thermopower exceeding $200~\mathrm{μV\,K^{-1}}$ for 900 nm wide and 30 $μ$m long electrodes, enabling precise detection of variations in the local temperature gradients. Exploiting this with CrPS$_4$ in a nonlocal geometry, we resolve distinct field dependent thermal conductivity changes associated with both the spin-flip and spin-flop magnetic transitions which we attribute to variations in the magnon$-$phonon coupling in CrPS$_4$. At 5 K, the transverse Seebeck response is modulated by more than 8$\%$ by an external magnetic field, demonstrating strong magnetic control of heat transport in CrPS$_4$. This all van der Waals platform offers high sensitivity to modulations of thermal conductivity and a broad adaptability to a wide range of exfoliated magnetic systems.

title: A KaiA Conformational Switch Links Day-Night Transitions to Clock Robustness
abstract: Biological clocks require mechanisms that enable transition between temporal phases and buffer against environmental fluctuations. In the cyanobacterial KaiABC-based circadian oscillator, KaiA has been regarded as a daytime activator that is passively sequestered at night. Here we define KaiA as a conformationally regulated activator and an active catalyst of the night-to-dawn transition. We identify a single linker helix, 5, that acts as a structural switch, mediating a domain-driven "tug-of-war" that sets the open-closed equilibrium in KaiA. Structure-guided mutations that shift this balance in either direction abolish stable rhythmicity both in vitro and in cells. Also, we show that substoichiometric KaiA dismantles nighttime KaiB-KaiC complexes through interactions with the KaiC C-terminal tails and likely initiates an autocatalytic feedback loop that resets the phosphorylation cycle at dawn. Furthermore, we present two independent kinetic models that offer distinct, deterministic explanations for the clock's low-temperature amplitude decline and failure at 20 {degrees} C.

title: A chemical perturbation scan on a K2P channel modulator pocket identifies affinity hotspots
abstract: Ion permeation in the two-pore-domain K+ (K2P) channel TREK1 is gated largely at the selectivity filter (SF), by a C-type-like inactivation mechanism involving distortions of the SF structure; and by a carbonyl flip, which disrupts K+ coordination. Both are prevented by a small-molecule activator bound adjacent to the SF, in a site termed the modulator pocket; yet which pocket regions carry the binding signal, and whether they couple to gating, is unclear. We use 46 chemical substitutions on the activator ML335, evaluated by non-equilibrium alchemical free-energy calculations, as an affinity perturbation scan on the lower- and upper pocket. The response is strongly asymmetric: Lower-ring substitutions impair binding, which we trace to a {pi}-{pi} stacking network connecting the M3, P2, P1 helices, and the SF. Conversely, upper-ring substitutions are tolerated and reshape contacts with the Cap-P1 and SF2-M4 loops; and with the upper SF. The identified affinity hotspots overlap with residues independently implicated in TREK gating by external cues such as pH, temperature, pressure, and cytosolic-sensor transduction, suggesting that high-affinity pocket sites might also shape the gating landscape.

title: LGALS3 Drives Dopamine Agonist Resistance in Prolactinoma by Activating the MAPK/ERK Pathway: A Multi-Omics Study
abstract: BackgroundDopamine agonist resistance is observed in 10%-30% of patients with prolactinomas, resulting in therapeutic failure and tumour progression. The molecular mechanisms underlying this resistance are not yet fully understood, highlighting the need for the identification of novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets.MethodsWe performed a comprehensive integrative analysis of bulk RNA sequencing and single-cell RNA sequencing datasets obtained from dopamine agonist-resistant and dopamine agonist-sensitive prolactinomas.

title: Redox Properties of the Copper Centers in Particulate Methane Monooxygenase
abstract: Particulate methane monooxygenase (pMMO) and its homolog ammonia monooxygenase (AMO), central enzymes in the global carbon and nitrogen cycles, contain three highly conserved mononuclear copper centers, denoted CuB, CuC, and CuD. While these sites have been well characterized structurally and spectroscopically, with recent studies identifying CuD as the active site, their reduction potentials have not been measured. This knowledge gap has hindered efforts to determine how the two electrons and two protons required for substrate oxidation are sourced and delivered.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: High-Harmonic Generation Probes Quantum Nuclear Fluctuations in Liquid Water
abstract: Nuclear quantum effects are essential for an accurate description of the hydrogen-bonded structure of liquid water, yet their spectroscopic signatures can be subtle and difficult to measure. Moreover, probing these effects in solution on femtosecond timescales (or below) is an open challenge that is pivotal for optical control of hydrogen bonds and ultrafast spectroscopy of proton transfer. Here, we combine path-integral molecular dynamics with real-time time-dependent density-functional theory to explore high-harmonic generation (HHG) in liquid water from first principles, rigorously accounting for quantum nuclear delocalisation. Relative to classical-nuclei simulations, quantum sampling suppresses the harmonic yield around certain harmonics by up to an order of magnitude, inducing local structural minima. By analysing the ab initio simulations and reproducing the key effects with a simplified model Hamiltonian, we trace the physical origins of the interference minima to the broadening of valence-band states induced by hydrogen-bond fluctuations, a mechanism expected to generalise to other hydrogen-bonded structures. Our work shows that nuclear quantum effects are indispensable for capturing ultrafast electronic dynamics in liquids, and demonstrates the power of liquid HHG spectroscopy for attosecond probing of nuclear fluctuations.

title: Learning Graph Energies for Finite-Time Generation
abstract: Energy-based models can represent distributions over discrete structures such as molecular graphs, but an energy that is accurate at equilibrium need not yield accurate samples when the sampler stops after a fixed number of steps. We introduce finite-horizon energy learning, which adapts the acceptance energy of a Metropolis--Hastings sampler to the distribution it returns after a prescribed number of steps, with initialization, proposals, and annealing schedule held fixed. For graph generation, a frozen pretrained model supplies initialization and proposals, and a learned energy governs acceptance. A training-only discriminator scores completed samples, and coupled continuations of the accepted and rejected branches of a proposal give an acceptance-gradient estimator that is unbiased for a fixed discriminator under stated conditions, without equilibrated negative samples or differentiation through discrete states. Generation uses the learned energy in the original single-trajectory sampler, without discriminator evaluations or reranking. On twelve pairwise binary targets with exactly evaluated terminal laws, learned energies have lower median terminal total variation than the equilibrium-correct energy in every tested short-horizon setting, and than its numerically tuned scalar multiple in most settings. On MOSES, a learned two-coefficient combination of pretrained Graph Energy Matching (GEM) potentials lowers FCD by 3.7--10.5\% relative to scale-calibrated GEM at matched sampling steps, with validity gains at the shortest budget and a sub-point validity trade-off at higher budgets.

title: MolHop: Scaffold-Hopping Molecular Design with Agentic Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Molecular design is often formulated as an optimization problem over existing molecular spaces. However, molecular optimization and the discovery of structurally distinct replacement molecules represent two fundamentally different search problems. LLM-based molecular design agents typically perform the former, conducting local refinement within the neighborhood of existing structures to improve target properties through structural modifications. In contrast, the latter requires exploration of a broader chemical space to discover molecules with entirely different scaffolds while preserving the functional characteristics of reference molecules. We propose MolHop, an agentic framework for cross-scaffold molecular discovery that enables models to navigate and edit within a pre-organized chemical space. MolHop organizes approximately 1.6 million molecular scaffolds from commercial molecules into a coarse-to-fine hierarchical action space. The agent selects new exploration regions through scaffold navigation actions and adjusts candidate properties through molecular editing. The framework maintains historical trajectory memory to support long-horizon search processes. On drug molecule and commercial compound tasks, connecting Grok-4.6 and DeepSeek-Flash-V4.1 to the MolHop framework substantially improves their cross-scaffold joint success rates. We develop MolHop-9B through agentic reinforcement learning, and MolHop-9B outperforms generative baselines including GPT-5.6-sol, Claude-5-Opus, and Gemini-3.1-Pro, while generating candidate molecules with larger scaffold differences from the reference molecules. These results demonstrate that effective molecular discovery beyond the traditional optimization paradigm requires structured chemical and action spaces, enabling agents to explore new structural regions rather than merely refine existing molecules.

title: Beyond DFT electronic band structures via dual-space orbital learning
abstract: Accurate electronic band structures are essential for predicting material properties, but high-fidelity calculations are computationally demanding. We introduce O-kRystal, a dual-space orbital-learning framework that uses a lower-cost Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) calculation as both an energy baseline and a source of structured orbital information. Combining PBE band energies with real- and reciprocal-space orbital matrices, O-kRystal predicts higher-level corrections for individual electronic states as a function of crystal momentum and spin. For states within 5 eV of the band-edge midpoint, it predicts Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof (HSE06) band energies with a mean absolute error of $0.171 \pm 0.009$ eV across nearly 6,000 three-dimensional materials spanning insulating, metallic, magnetic, and nonmagnetic systems. On a separate benchmark of six strongly correlated materials, it reduces the corresponding PBE band-energy MAE by 68.7% and resolves orbital-dependent changes in the relative placement of transition-metal d and ligand p states. Despite training only at high-symmetry points, it maintains comparable accuracy at unseen points along band paths and reconstructs HSE06 densities of states from dense Brillouin-zone predictions. Finally, training O-kRystal on $G_0W_0$ quasiparticle energies for two-dimensional materials demonstrates its applicability across levels of theory and the potential of orbital learning for higher-fidelity, momentum-resolved electronic-structure prediction beyond density functional theory.

title: Tailoring Superhydrophobic Ultramicropores in Covalent Organic Frameworks for Humidity-Resistant Methane Purification
abstract: Efficient purification of methane from raw natural gas under humid conditions remains challenging because water adsorption often degrades the separation performance and structural stability of porous adsorbents. Here we report a topology- and stacking-guided molecular design strategy that integrates ultramicropore engineering with pore-surface fluorination to construct superhydrophobic covalent organic frameworks (COFs) for humidity-resistant methane purification.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Unlocking the Tertiary Nitrogen Effect in 3D Anisotropic Covalent Organic Frameworks to Achieve Record Iodine Capture under Industrial Conditions
abstract: Using porous adsorbents to achieve efficient capture of radioactive iodine from nuclear waste under industrial conditions remains a formidable challenge, since most adsorbents just exhibit a low iodine uptake under such conditions. We herein show two 3D [8 + 4]-assembled covalent organic frameworks (COFs, ECUT-COF-99 and ECUT-COF-100) for this challenging target. The two COFs feature a minimal-transitivity [3 4] flu-derived net, which allows anisotropic isoreticular expansion through a general sequential derived-net approach.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: A Predictive Framework Integrating Network Toxicology and Machine Learning Elucidates 6PPD-Quinone-Induced Glioblastoma Pathogenesis
abstract: Objective This article aims to systematically explore the molecular mechanism of glioblastoma induced by 6PPD-Q. Methods Differential expression analysis and weighted gene co-expression network analysis were conducted on five independent GBM transcriptome datasets in the NCBI GEO database. It is used to identify the function-related gene modules related to the pathogenesis of GBM. This paper employs three complementary computational methods, to predict the possible protein targets of 6PPD-Q. This paper adopts machine learning algorithms to identify the core diagnostic genes.

title: Magnetic tunnel junctions of twisted La2/3Sr1/3MnO3 freestanding bilayers
abstract: Transition metal oxides (TMOs) host a variety of emergent spintronic or multiferroic functionalities owing to the intricate interplay between lattice, orbital, charge, and spin degrees of freedom. Recent advances in epitaxial lift-off and dry transfer techniques using water-soluble sacrificial layers enables stacking and twisting of freestanding membranes of such strongly correlated oxides, providing even richer physical properties and functionalities. To date, the twisted junctions of TMOs have been mainly investigated in insulators, focusing on their structural and dielectric properties. Here, we demonstrate that the twisted bilayer membranes of La2/3Sr1/3MnO3, a prototypical half-metallic ferromagnetic metal TMO, offer a magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ) with their van der Waals (vdW) gap acting as a tunnel barrier. The twisted junctions of La2/3Sr1/3MnO3 exhibit tunnelling magnetoresistance (TMR) effect with respect to relative orientation of magnetizations of top and bottom membranes. In addition, high-field magnetoresistance shows uniaxial anisotropy, which can be assigned to tunnelling anisotropic magnetoresistance (TAMR) effect reflecting rhombohedral distortion of fully-relaxed La2/3Sr1/3MnO3. The demonstration of TMR and TAMR effects suggests that spin and in-plane momentum degrees of freedom of 3d electrons are conserved across the twisted junctions of TMOs, opening a new avenue for realizing strongly correlated twistronics utilizing electron coherence through tunnelling processes.

title: Intercalation of Ultrathin Ferromagnetic Iron Films at the Graphene/SiC Interface
abstract: The intercalation of high-quality PASG-grown (polymer-assisted sublimation growth) zero-layer graphene on 4H-SiC(0001) with iron is studied using a deposition-and-annealing approach. We find that unlike other metals, Fe does not easily intercalate, and the intercalation procedure has to be balanced with the formation of iron silicides and graphitic carbon at the interface. After successful intercalation, the ultrathin iron films are protected against oxidation by the covering graphene sheet, and retain ferromagnetic behaviour with an in-plane easy axis even at room temperature. When exposed to a selenium-rich atmosphere at elevated temperatures, an almost complete exchange of Fe by Se is observed, imposing a major restriction for the formation of multi-element 2D compounds via sequential intercalation schemes.

title: Curvature-driven passive mixing in three-dimensional conical helix micromixers
abstract: Passive microfluidic mixing is fundamentally constrained by the dominance of laminar flow, a limitation commonly addressed using embedded obstacles or surface modifications, often at the cost of increased fabrication complexity and hydraulic resistance. Here, we introduce a conical helix micromixer (CHM) that combines circular and helical microchannel topologies into a monolithic geometry capable of passively generating progressively intensified Dean vortices through continuously varying curvature. This curvature-driven mechanism induces strong transverse transport and achieves a mixing index (MI) > 95% in the first turn of the CHM across varying flow rates (1-2500 µL min-1) without requiring any internal roughness structures or external energy inputs, as validated by field-based mixing simulations. A central methodological contribution is a reduced-order planar representation of the full three-dimensional (3D) CHM geometry for flow-field analysis and optimization. Direct geometrical validation against the original 3D conical-helix centreline demonstrated projection-induced deviations below 2% across all investigated configurations, with most cases remaining below 1%, confirming that the planar representation preserves the dominant geometric characteristics of the true 3D flow path with negligible loss of fidelity. This reduced-order strategy lowered computational costs by approximately an order of magnitude, while preserving a strong correlation with full 3D field-based calculations across the investigated ranges of Reynolds numbers. Geometric and flow parameters were systematically explored using a Taguchi framework, while gradient-boosted machine-learning models were employed as mechanistic analytical tools to quantify parameter sensitivity. Both analyses consistently identified the inlet curvature radius as the dominant design variable governing Dean vortex onset and mixing-length compression, with tighter curvature significantly accelerating the development of transverse mixing. The results prove that controlled curvature modulation alone can function as an efficient passive mixing engine, providing a compact, fabrication-ready platform for microreactor synthesis, point-of-care diagnostics, and scalable lab-on-a-chip applications.

title: Imaging of Electrochemically Programmed Single-Molecule Reactions
abstract: Single-molecule reactions reveal intrinsic heterogeneity that is obscured in ensemble measurements. However, most existing approaches rely on extreme dilution, ultrasmall solution volumes, or physical confinement to keep individual events sufficiently sparse. Here, we introduce electrochemically programmed single-molecule reactions (PSMR), a pulse-regulated strategy that shifts single-molecule electrochemistry from passive observation to active control. It converts continuous interfacial reactions to a sequence of short, repeatable reaction trials.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Reactivity and Selectivity of Photocatalytic Nitrate Reduction Reaction to Ammonia: Pt, Pd, Ir, and Rh Single Atoms on p-Type TiO2 Nanotubes
abstract: We present a systematic study of noble metal (Pt, Pd, Ir, and Rh) single-atom cocatalysts decorated on p-type and quantum-confined TiO2 nanotubes for photocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia. All single-atom cocatalysts were prepared through a reactive deposition using different metal precursors, resulting in a single-atom oxidation state (δ+) of δ ≈ 2. At a similar loading concentration (0.2–0.3 at%) and in the absence of any sacrificial agent, Pd single atoms exhibit the highest element-specific activity for ammonia production, while Pt single atoms display a prominent photocatalytic activity with a strong tendency of nitrite reduction toward ammonia. Rh single atoms achieve the highest ammonia selectivity, whereas Ir single atoms predominantly produce nitrite due to inhibited subsequent reduction. Comparisons with single atoms deposited on conventional TiO2 (P25) and with nanoparticles supported on the nanotubes reveal that both the semiconductor properties (quantum confinement effect and p-type conductivity) and the speciation of the cocatalyst (single atom) can significantly enhance activity and selectivity. These findings aid in establishing design principles for different single-atom catalysts toward efficient and selective photocatalytic nitrogen valorization.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: MASON: Materials Atomistic Structure builder Operated in Natural language
abstract: Building reliable atomistic models is a critical and often challenging step in first-principles calculations. Although large language model agents can assist with structure generation, they lack direct capabilities for crystallographic operations and therefore struggle to construct complex structures reliably. Here we present MASON, an AI-native toolkit for atomistic structure construction that can be invoked by agents through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). In an end-to-end example, an agent builds a CO/Pt(111) adsorption model from a natural language request. By equipping agents with dedicated structure-building tools, MASON enables reliable and efficient atomistic model construction and provides a foundation for autonomous first-principles workflows.

title: Andreev-reflection spectroscopy of SrPt3P single crystals
abstract: The interplay between inversion symmetry breaking and superconducting pairing mechanisms is a long-standing puzzle of solid-state physics. Ternary platinum phosphide SrPt$_3$P is an excellent case study in this regard, since it shares the distorted anti-perovskite crystal structure of non-centrosymmetric superconductor CePt$_3$Si but preserves the inversion symmetry center, enabling a direct comparison between the two compounds. Despite intense scrutiny, the superconducting pairing strength, gap symmetry, and magnitude of SrPt$_3$P remain an open question. Here, we study the gap structure of high-quality SrPt$_3$P single crystals with $T_c = 8.6$ K by using point-contact Andreev-reflection spectroscopy. The spectra systematically showed symmetric conductance maxima and a zero-bias minimum, as is typical of fully gapped superconductors, and dips at finite voltage $V_\mathrm{dip}$ due to the local transition of the contact region to the resistive state. In contacts with high resistance, where the dips fall sufficiently far from the gap features, the conductance curves can be well fitted with a single isotropic $s$-wave gap. The temperature dependence $Δ(T)$ of the gap amplitude extracted from the fit is in good agreement with the one predicted by the BCS theory, with a zero-temperature mean value $Δ(0)=1.88\pm0.08$ meV, and a mean gap ratio $2Δ/k_\mathrm{B}T_c = 5.2\pm0.2$.

title: Quantifying the Spin–Optical Properties of Bent π-Carbene Molecular Qubits
abstract: Through spin-selective intersystem crossings (ISCs) among photoexcited electronic states, organic π-diradicals can be spin-polarized by optical excitation, positioning them as long-lived, tunable, and scalable qubits. Recent advancements have utilized triplet π-carbenes of bent structures, which unlock an additional spin-selective ISC channel between the ground states, improving the qubit’s spin–optical properties. However, bent π-carbenes also lose spin selectivity in the excited-state ISC step and a compromise has yet to be found.
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: Recognition Loop Dynamics Differentiates m6A-mRNA Reader Domains of YTHDF Proteins
abstract: The three human YTH-domain family proteins (YTHDF1, YTHDF2, and YTHDF3) are highly homologous and recognize the N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification of mRNA with essentially identical binding modes and affinities. This homogeneity challenges the well-established view that different YTHDF proteins play distinct cellular functions (the specificity view), with an emerging argument that these proteins may instead play redundant roles.
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: Machine learning in placental research: a review and guide for future studies
abstract: Machine learning approaches are increasingly applied across biomedical research to analyze complex, high-dimensional datasets and identify patterns that may inform disease diagnosis and biological discovery. In reproductive and placental research, these methods are used to investigate fetal development, pregnancy complications, and early-life health outcomes using molecular and clinical data. Machine learning approaches have widely been applied to placental and obstetric imaging, such as ultrasound, although these applications have been extensively reviewed elsewhere.

title: Modeling electrodeposition of thin films with compact, dendritic, and random morphologies
abstract: We summarize previously published computer simulation studies of a metal electrodeposition model that considers diffusive cation flux, a fast reaction in contact with the electrode or with the growing deposit, and adsorbed atom diffusion in finite time windows. Simulations with various parameters show compact, fractal, dendritic deposits, and dynamic transitions between different morphologies during the growth of individual samples. The dendritic shapes are characterized by hierarchical organizations in which branches of a given order reproduce the shape and crystalline orientation of the branches of the previous order, in contrast to the random branching of the fractal deposits formed by DLA and related models. The simulations show dendrites with maple leaf shape in SC lattices, pine tree shape in FCC lattices, and flower-like shape in HCP lattices, with surfaces predominantly oriented in the lowest-energy configurations of each lattice. Simulations with nucleation restricted to a nanoscale seed show the initial formation of faceted particles followed by dendrite formation, in agreement with silver electrodeposition on substrates patterned with gold nanoparticles. A quantitative application to faceted and dendritic silver obtained in the same experiment provides values of the model parameters which are consistent with the characteristic widths of these structures being of the same order of magnitude of the diffusion lengths of atoms on (111) and (001) surfaces. Using an extended model for iron electrodeposition on Si(100), the simulations qualitatively reproduce the initial formation of multilayer islands, small oscillations of the roughness of a polycrystalline compact film after island coalescence, and instability development. Possible directions for applying this modeling to the electrodeposition of other materials are suggested.

title: From scrap to prime: Designing high-performance alloys from dirty feedstocks with machine learning
abstract: Producing alloys from recycled metals via secondary synthesis can markedly cut energy use, greenhouse-gas emissions, and dependence on scarce, strategically important elements relative to primary routes. The central obstacle is the feedstock itself: Scrap is chemically heterogeneous and unpredictable, a "dirty" mix whose impurities typically embrittle materials. Conventional strategies address this challenge by diluting impurities through the addition of virgin material, thereby restricting scrap utilization, limiting microstructural design freedom, and undermining cost and sustainability benefits. Here, we introduce a fundamentally different, data-driven paradigm that deliberately reverses a five-millennia-old metallurgical injunction: Rather than purifying the alloy, we design the alloy to accommodate and exploit its contaminants. Using a model ductile iron representative of 120 million metric tons of heavily contaminated scrap, we couple experiments with deep-neural-network optimization to identify chemically robust, impurity-tolerant processing windows. The resulting "dirty" irons retain ductility and strength by integrating impurity effects into a purposeful microstructure, rather removing them. The approach achieves complete recyclability, an 8.1% reduction in manufacturing cost, and mechanical gains of up to 15.2% in ultimate tensile strength and 73.2% in elongation at fracture. Crucially, it overcomes the canonical strength-ductility trade-off while enabling far greater scrap utilization and material circularity. By endowing alloys with a practical "gene of scrap compatibility," this strategy reframes alloy design for a resource-constrained future and advances a mass-conserving circular economy for metals.

title: Using artificial intelligence in your job search
authors: Brought to you by ACS Careers

title: CAS and Novartis collaborate to advance access to reaction data and AI research
abstract: Researchers will gain access to integrated proprietary experimental reaction data to be used with the CAS Content Collection

title: Asymmetric Elongation of Uranyl within a Silver Nanocluster
abstract: Confinement within nanoscale cavities can profoundly alter molecular structure and electronic properties, but this strategy has never been applied to inherently linear and symmetric uranyl cations (UO22+). Here, we report the first example of uranyl encapsulation within a self-assembled silver nanocluster, [UO2F5@Ag21(CCBut)14](BF4)3F (CCBut = 3,3-dimethyl-1-butynyl), abbreviated as UO2F5@Ag21. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction reveals asymmetric elongation of the axial O ≡ U≡O bonds from the ideal symmetric value of 1.77 Å to 1.788(9) and 1.837(9) Å, respectively.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Beyond SELEX: AI-driven aptamers from sequence to structure to function
abstract: Conventional aptamer discovery by systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX) is often constrained by limited library capacity, PCR bias, and multi-round screening. The recent convergence of artificial intelligence with aptamer development is driving a paradigm shift from empirical screening toward rational, data-driven design. This Review presents a timely and comprehensive overview of AI integration across the entire aptamer development pipeline, with a particular emphasis on advances reported in 2024-2026.

title: Sparse Phosphorylatable Residues, Tuned by Agonist Chemotype, Shapes GPCR Signaling
abstract: GPCR signaling diversity is often attributed to an intracellular phosphorylation barcode, in which ligand-dependent modification of multiple receptor phosphoresidues encodes selective engagement of downstream transducers. However, whether such an extensive phosphorylation of the receptor is universally required remains unclear. Here, we show that the melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R), a central regulator of energy homeostasis, achieves remarkably diverse and pathway-selective signaling through a sparse set of strategically positioned regulatory phosphoresidues.

title: Generative design of functional disordered regions in a developmental transcription factor
abstract: Rapid advances in protein structure design have not translated to intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). This is largely due to our incomplete understanding of how IDR sequence encodes function. Here, we use stem cell differentiation as a model to map functional sequence features in the IDR of transcription factor RUNX2. We show that RUNX2 requires its C-terminal IDR to bind chromatin and regulate gene expression during osteogenesis. Surprisingly, linear IDR sequence is dispensable, and instead features of the conformational ensemble predict function.

title: Periodic Graphics: What are phone screens made from?
abstract: Chemical educator and Compound Interest blogger Andy Brunning examines the materials that give phone screens strength, color, and touch sensitivity

title: Dehydration-Responsive Left-Handed G-Quadruplexes Expandthe Sequence Repertoire
abstract: G-quadruplexes (G4s) are widely studied noncanonical nucleic-acid structures that carry important biological functions. Typically, G4s form from G-rich sequences containing at least four tracts of more than two consecutive guanines, yet a plethora of unconventional G4-forming sequences have been identified, including sequences that fold into G4s only under specific conditions. These G4 states remain poorly resolved. Here we identify dehydration-responsive left-handed G4s (drLHG4s), a class of left-handed G4 (LHG4) structures accessible under dehydrating conditions. Using d(GT)n repeats, we show that left-handed folding depends on repeat length, salt condition and solvent conditions. Systematic mutational analysis reveals a broader but register-constrained sequence space, while high-resolution crystal structures of d-GTGGTGTGTGGTG, a sequence that folded robustly under dehydrating conditions, establish a bulged LHG4 architecture and reveal a distinctive hydration sphere. We further show that selected peptides and a cationic zinc phthalocyanine derivative, ZnTEGQPyrPc, containing four triethylene glycol methyl ether tails can induce LHG4 states. Together, our findings reveal a dehydration-responsive G4 landscape and expand the experimentally accessible sequence space of LHG4 folding.

title: Evaluation of Murrayanine's anticancer potential in breast cancer: Integrative computational, in vitro, and nanoparticle delivery approaches
abstract: Breast cancer continues to be a major threat to women's health on a global scale. Innovative treatments that are effective and well-tolerated are greatly needed. Nature-derived compounds, such as phytochemicals, have gained widespread interest owing to their diverse anti-tumor actions on cancer cells. Murrayanine, found in Murraya koenigii, has shown efficacy as an anticancer agent by promoting apoptosis, inducing reactive oxygen species, and regulating pivotal pathways like PI3K/Akt and NF-κB.
venue: The Journal of steroid biochemistry and molecular biology

title: DiffuChannel: A Conditional Denoising Diffusion Model that Synthesises Single-Molecule Patch-Clamp Data with Exactly Known Idealisation (Ground Truth)
abstract: Development of computational models for single-channel patch-clamp analysis is hampered by limited availability of labelled (idealised) data. Since experiment alone cannot provide a genuine ground truth, two simulation methods are commonly employed; Stochastic sampling from a specified Markov model, augmented with synthetic noise allows creation of unlimited, flawlessly idealised/annotated datasets, yet its authenticity hinges entirely on the premises underlying data and noise generation. A more recent method uses GAN-based generation, this also replicates real-world noise and artefacts, but does not include a ground truth idealisation or annotation and training is notoriously unstable. Here, we introduce DiffuChannel, a conditional noise-removal diffusion model that addresses these drawbacks. Channel dynamics come directly from a user-defined discrete-time Markov chain (or a model fitted to biological seed data), thus, the state assignment for each synthetic trace is precisely determined by design. The diffusion model is then trained exclusively to capture the noise distribution of raw current conditioned on a given idealisation, thereby replicating genuine noise, filtering, and artefact patterns observed in real data without needing to hand craft noise models. We use a two-step coarse-to-fine workflow that starts with a defined slow-envelope component conditioned on longer-term dwell-time features extracted from the input idealisation. This allows a degree of baseline drift and time-dependent relaxations to be captured over timescales far longer than the network's field of view. At generation time, we use a context-preserving inpainting method that enables creation of relatively seamless traces of any desired duration. We demonstrate that with only a limited set of labelled seed traces, synthetic records yield realistic all-points amplitude distribution, noise power spectrum, autocorrelation pattern, and slow envelope comparable to the source data. The model achieves a maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between windowed real and generated data of 0.005 (median across the five phenotypes). This compares to a within real-split-half MMD value of 0.002 and an amplitude-matched white noise MMD value of 0.108. In this paper, we benchmark this against DeepGANnel. Since the underlying Markov model is defined rather than estimated, DiffuChannel generates infinite, perfectly labelled, phenotype-consistent training data ideal for developing and testing idealisation algorithms. We find that, in practice, this new method is far more stable than previous GAN models and runs start to end without human intervention. We provide the model open-source along with an interactive web-based training and synthesis interface/app.

title: MolLean: A Process-Verifiable Language for Chemical Reasoning
abstract: Chemical chain-of-thought can contain hallucinated structural and property claims. We thereby introduce MolLean, a process-verifiable language that grounds chemical reasoning in an explicit molecular state. A layered Lean-based kernel checks state transitions and assertions over molecular readouts, from primitive graph edits to compound transformations. Meanwhile, a typed witness protocol separates native structural checks from externally supplied measurements. We further introduce MolLean-MCP, a stateful tool interface that exposes these transitions, checks, and readouts during generation: the model receives feedback to decide its next action, and rejected actions leave the state unchanged. MolLean supports one-pass trace execution, whole-trace refinement, and interactive reasoning through MolLean-MCP. We evaluate these three modes with direct chain-of-thought on 8,800 matched examples across 12 tasks spanning molecular generation, editing, optimization, and reactions. With Qwen3.6-27B, whole-trace refinement outperforms direct chain-of-thought on all 12 tasks. MolLean-MCP complements whole-trace refinement with stepwise verification feedback, reaching better performance in reaction tasks. Together, these results highlight an executable foundation for chemical reasoning, in which explicit chemical commitments can be checked and revised rather than remaining solely in free-form explanations.

title: Cartesian and Curvilinear Anharmonic Frequencies and Intensities: Perturb-then-Diagonalize Polyad Transport and Adiabatic Discrete-Variable Representation
abstract: Anharmonic intensities reveal vibrational coupling that band positions alone cannot determine. We derive explicit second-order infrared transition moments in curvilinear normal coordinates, including kinetic metric derivatives and transport through variational resonance polyads. The vibrational perturbation-to-second-order-then-diagonalization (VP2TD) treatment covers fundamentals, overtones, three-quantum transitions, and hot bands. A general computational platform combines Extended Symmetry-Adapted Local Coordinates (ESALCs), using Cartesian (ESALC-C) or internal (ESALC-I) primitives, with interchangeable quantum-chemical programs and parallel finite differences. Independent oscillator matrices verify the intensity equations; a molecular water check reproduces second-order amplitudes within $8.4\times10^{-8}$ atomic units. Comparisons with established tools reproduce a formaldehyde Fermi polyad within 0.163 cm$^{-1}$ and 0.061 km mol$^{-1}$ and water Raman activities within $10^{-7}$ Angstrom$^6$. For 29 matched formaldehyde rotational line pairs, the predicted hot-to-fundamental intensity ratio, using the measured lower-state energy, is consistent with the nuclear-spin-corrected median: the differences are 3.9% (ESALC-I) and 3.8% (ESALC-C), compared with a 15% uncertainty estimate for individual measured line intensities. Common analytic reference derivatives ensure identical harmonic observables, while internal coordinates reduce and localize intermode anharmonic couplings. Rotation-vibration constants extend the same tensor treatment. An integrated adiabatic discrete-variable representation treats large-amplitude motions, and finite-level partition functions provide anharmonic thermochemistry.

title: Structural identification in general crystalline systems via Voronoi cell topology
abstract: Widely used methods for identifying crystal structure in atomistic simulations are limited in practice to a handful of simple structures, leaving many important crystalline systems without automated classification techniques. Voronoi topology analysis offers a route to classifying arbitrary crystalline and defect environments, but realizing this potential first requires enumerating the Voronoi cell topologies that can arise under thermal perturbation of a structure of interest. We present an algorithm that deterministically enumerates all Voronoi cell topologies arising from generic infinitesimal perturbations of an arbitrary crystal structure, producing structural classifiers that extend automated identification to general crystalline systems. We demonstrate the approach on several structures of general interest.

title: Structure–Redox–Magnetism Dynamics Induced by Pd–Fe Interaction in Mixed Iron Oxide Nanoparticles
abstract: The incorporation of noble metals into iron oxide nanomaterials represents an effective strategy to tailor their redox and structural properties through metal-oxide interactions. However, a detailed experimental understanding of these effects is limited. This work investigates the impact of Pd incorporation and Ag perturbation in mixed iron oxide nanoparticles by combining bulk- and surface-sensitive techniques. X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) shows that Pd significantly enhances iron reducibility. Accordingly, wavelet transform analysis of the EXAFS region further provides evidence of Fe–Pd interactions, indicating nanoscale proximity between Pd and Fe atoms. These bulk-sensitive results are complemented by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), which reveals an increased fraction of reduced Fe species at the nanoparticle near surface upon Pd incorporation. In situ grazing-incidence X-ray diffraction (GI-XRD) during heat treatment under H2 provides insight into the evolution of these effects, showing (i) suppression of the hematite minor phase already after Pd impregnation and (ii) magnetite major phase lattice expansion during H2 treatment, both occurring exclusively in the presence of Pd. Complementary XPS analysis indicates partial migration of Pd into the iron oxide lattice under H2 treatment, contributing to the oxide lattice expansion beyond that of iron reduction alone. Magnetic measurements reveal an overall magnetization increase upon Pd incorporation, with a nonlinear dependence on Pd loading reflecting the balance between enhanced iron reducibility and lattice disorder. Finally, Ag incorporation slightly increases the fraction of reduced Fe species but strongly alters the magnetic response, consistent with an additional bimetallic perturbation arising from Pd–Ag coexistence.

title: Balancing composition and phase stability in High-Entropy Metal Phosphates for proton conduction
abstract: The transition to sustainable energy technologies necessitates the development of proton-conducting electrolytes free from critical raw materials. Transition metal phosphate octahydrates (vivanite and pakhmoskyite analogues) offer a promising structural platform for proton transport via the vehicle mechanism, yet their performance is typically dominated by specific cation identity, with cobalt-based systems serving as the benchmark.

title: Multi-Objective Molecular Generation via Actor-Critic Regulated by Adaptive Cooperative Evolution
abstract: Many complex diseases involve intricate and interdependent biological mechanisms, making multi-target drug design therapeutically important. However, existing molecular generation models often struggle to balance conflicting property requirements, maintain structural exploration, and avoid premature convergence during reinforcement learning. To address these challenges, we propose CMIR-RL, a reinforcement learning-based molecular generation model that integrates cooperative crossover-mutation exploration, structure-based intrinsic rewards, and Pareto-based multi-objective optimization.
venue: IEEE transactions on computational biology and bioinformatics

title: Relationship between serum cotinine and risk of tooth loss in adults: A comprehensive statistical framework and molecular mechanisms
abstract: This study aimed to investigate the association between serum cotinine (a tobacco exposure biomarker) and tooth loss risk in adults. This study employed a statistical framework incorporating logistic regression, restricted cubic spline (RCS), machine learning, and web page construction to investigate the association between serum cotinine levels and tooth loss in 12,559 adult National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey participants. Network pharmacology was used to identify key targets, whereas molecular docking explored the specific mechanism of cotinine's impact on the target protein.

title: Growth-induced trade-off between polarity, electrical isolation, and structural quality in AlN grown on Si(111) by plasma-assisted molecular beam epitaxy
abstract: We investigate the effects of substrate temperature and Al flux, at a fixed N flux, on the polarity, electrical properties, and structural quality of AlN films grown on high-resistivity Si(111) by plasma-assisted molecular beam epitaxy. N-rich conditions result in relatively highly resistive Al-polar AlN/Si, whereas Al-rich conditions promote N-polarity and improved structural quality but simultaneously lead to increased p-type conductivity of AlN/Si stacks, consistent with unintentional Al doping of the Si substrate during AlN growth. Increasing the substrate temperature further improves the structural quality while enhancing the unwanted conductivity, revealing a growth-induced trade-off among polarity, electrical isolation, and structural quality. By reducing the substrate temperature to 575°C while maintaining slightly Al-rich conditions, an N-polar AlN/Si stack with a sheet resistance of 276 kΩ/sq is achieved. These results provide guidelines for optimizing AlN/Si templates for various nitride device heterostructures.

title: Exchange Interactions and Magnon Spectra in bcc Fe(001) Thin Films: A Computational Study
abstract: We combined density functional theory with atomistic spin dynamics to understand how surfaces influence magnon dispersion. For this purpose, we investigate thin layers of body-centered cubic iron and compare them with the bulk material. We present how the broken symmetry affects exchange interactions and magnon behavior. Our results reveal enhanced magnetic moments and exchange interactions for surface atoms compared to bulk Fe. The increase in exchange interaction integrals is mostly visible for first- and second-nearest neighbors. We also find a significant spread in exchange values within each coordination shell. Magnon dispersion analysis shows, for the layered system, pronounced band blurring, a significant reduction of maximum frequencies relative to the previously reported bulk values, and the emergence of a low-frequency band outside the \g{}-point. Our study shows that relying on bulk exchange parameters introduces errors in the magnon spectra of ultrathin systems, underscoring the need for a detailed, system-specific approach.

title: Landau quantization of $C_3$ high-fold fermions in honeycomb lattices
abstract: We present the theory of the Landau levels of $C_3$ high-fold fermions in honeycomb lattices. These fermions arise as a generalization of the tight-binding model in a honeycomb lattice with one orbital per site, known to describe graphene, to a family of models with several orbitals per site transforming according to representations of $C_3$, relevant for triangulene two-dimensional crystals. The models are defined by the number of orbitals $n_a$ and $n_b$ at the $a$ and $b$ sites of the unit cell. They feature energy bands that combine flat bands and Dirac cones, that are isomorphic to those of graphene, the Lieb, $p_{xy}$ honeycomb, and the Kagome tight-binding models. Combining tight-binding and $k\cdot p$ methods, here we compute the Landau levels of the $(1,1)$, $(1,2)$, $(2,2)$ and $(3,3)$ models, we compare them to those of the reference models, and we explore the similarities and differences with the Landau levels in graphene. Our findings reveal that the nature of $C_3$ high-fold fermions combine Dirac-type Landau quantization, originating from the linear crossings and associated relativistic band dispersion, with anomalous Landau quantization rooted in the quantum geometry of the singular flat bands.

title: Redox-Induced Polymeric Micelle-to-Coacervate Transition for Enhanced Endosomal Escape, Prolonged Drug Retention, and Improved Sequential Drug Delivery
abstract: Polymeric micelles (PMs) and coacervate microdroplets (CMs) are both promising delivery vehicles, yet each suffers from distinct limitations. The delivery efficiency of PMs is often hindered by factors, such as limited endosome escape and uncontrolled drug release. On the other hand, CMs are prone to coalescence and aging, which hamper long-term storage and systemic injection. Here, by employing an intracellular morphological transition strategy, these drawbacks can be efficiently addressed without compromising their inherent advantages.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Coordination-Controlled Stability of Pd Single-Atom Catalysts under Electrochemical Conditions
abstract: Single-atom catalysts (SACs) maximize atom utilization and site-specificity for diverse chemical and electrochemical transformations. While activity and selectivity have been optimized through advanced synthetic methods, the electrochemical stability of SACs remains insufficiently understood and limits practical application. Here, we employ operando inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) to quantify the dissolution kinetics of palladium (Pd) SACs in acidic electrolyte across a wide potential window. Operando electrochemically coupled mass spectrometry (EC-MS) confirms concurrent carbon support corrosion. By systematically varying heteroatom dopants, applied potentials, electrolyte pH, and adsorbing anions, we decouple coordination-driven (intrinsic) and electrochemical (extrinsic) factors controlling metal leaching. Specifically, the external potential exhibits a more pronounced influence on the stability of Pd SACs, while the coordinating heteroatoms modulate stability through both direct interaction with the isolated Pd centers and influence on the carbon support. Complementary X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) reveal dynamic restructuring of the Pd coordination environment, linking local chemical structure to macroscopic stability. These results provide mechanistic insights into SAC degradation pathways and establish design principles for stable single-atom architectures in energy conversion applications.

title: Machine learning models identify a distinct urinary metabolomic signature in children with non-systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis
abstract: ObjectivesDespite advances in understanding the molecular mechanisms behind juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), reliable non-invasive biomarkers for diagnosis and monitoring remain limited. Urinary metabolomics offers a promising approach to investigate disease-specific metabolic alterations, especially in the paediatric setting. This exploratory study aimed to characterise the urinary metabolomic profile of children with non-systemic JIA with a machine learning-based approach.MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional study including 98 participants under 18 years of age (58 non-systemic JIA…

title: Crystallization of the undertile
abstract: We classify all periodic tilings with a monotile known as $\mathbf{R1}$ and called here the undertile, which underlies several aperiodic monotiles such as the Taylor-Socolar one. The classification is done using deflation, through a study of fracture lines between zones where deflation can be performed. A full classification of fracture patterns is given, that also applies to non-periodic tilings with the undertile. This can be used to reprove non-periodicity of some existing monotiles based on the undertile.

title: Counterfactual Neighborhood Risk Fields: Evidence-Grounded Selective Safety for Vision-Language Models
abstract: Representation-based safety defenses for vision-language models (VLMs) often learn to separate harmful from benign inputs, but separation alone does not establish what a risk score means or when it should be trusted. We introduce Counterfactual Neighborhood Risk Fields (CNRF), an evidence-grounded framework for selective VLM safety. CNRF constructs context-matched benign-harmful counterfactual pairs, uses their representation differences as capability-related risk directions, and estimates neighborhood support separately from risk. This separation prevents unfamiliarity from being conflated with harmfulness and enables selective intervention rather than blanket rejection. A victim-adaptive interface accommodates different safety observations across VLM architectures and routes selected requests for same-victim response review, which either releases acceptable candidates or produces constrained alternatives with reduced harmful capability. Across three VLMs and five multimodal jailbreak families, CNRF achieves 86.06-89.30% macro defense success rate while retaining substantial benign-task utility. Controlled experiments further show that query-matched references and preserved context-direction correspondence materially improve risk ranking in the low-false-positive regime. CNRF thus reframes representation-based VLM safety from learning harmfulness boundaries to constructing applicable evidence for selective risk decisions.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Rapid Diagnostics for Antimicrobial Resistance: From Bench to Bedside
abstract: BackgroundAntimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one of the most urgent global public health threats, especially in low- and middle-income countries. In 2019, bacterial AMR was estimated to have directly caused approximately 1.27 million deaths and to have been associated with 4.95 million deaths worldwide. Rapid identification of resistant infections is important, yet established diagnostics are very slow. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has revolutionized microbiology and infectious disease diagnostics. This review explores the space of AI-enabled diagnostics for AMR detection and characterization.MethodsThis literature review was conducted from January to September 2026 using PubMed/MEDLINE, Google Scholar, and other electronic databases with keywords including "AI," "AMR," "deep learning," "genomic diagnostics," and "point-of-care (POC) testing." Following screening and full-text assessment, 67 Peer-reviewed articles and systematic reviews were included to support the synthesis presented in the manuscript, while non-peer-reviewed articles and studies lacking direct AI relevance were excluded. Titles and abstracts were screened before full-text review.ResultsAI-enhanced diagnostics were reported to shorten turnaround time for AMR detection with promising but heterogeneous predictive performance; for example, pooled estimates across antimicrobial stewardship applications indicate an area under the curve of approximately 0.72. They also support improving antimicrobial stewardship and enable early therapeutic optimization in laboratory and POC settings, enabling real-time clinical decision-making. Despite these achievements, evidence for direct improvements in patient outcomes and routine bedside effectiveness remains limited.ConclusionAI-driven diagnostic tools represent a promising strategy to bridge laboratory innovation and bedside application in combating AMR. The tools have the capacity to improve patient outcomes and enhance antimicrobial stewardship as they can accurately detect resistance patterns and support real-time clinical decisions. However, long-term sustainability, long-term success, and global impact can be achieved by continued validation, regulatory alignment, and equitable implementation across diverse healthcare settings.

title: Molecular Insights into the Collagen-binding Specificity of Discoidin Domain Receptors
abstract: Discoidin domain receptors, DDR1 and DDR2, are a subfamily of homologous receptor tyrosine kinases that are activated by the extracellular matrix (ECM) collagens. Together the two DDRs recognize at least seven of the twenty-eight known collagen types (Col1-28) with distinct specificities. For example, Col1-3 and Col5 that exist as fibres in connective tissues activate both DDRs whereas Col6 microfilaments found in ECM of skeletal muscles preferentially activates DDR1. Further, Col4 found in basement membrane as mesh-like networks preferentially activates DDR1 but similarly network-forming Col10 abundant in cartilage preferentially binds and activates DDR2. These preferential interactions activate specific signalling pathways driving distinct physiological processes and pathologies, yet their molecular basis is currently not understood. Here, we show that the collagen-binding specificity of the DDRs is determined by electrostatic interactions at the receptor-ligand binding interface. The collagen-binding site in the two DDRs differ in the nature and placement of electrostatically charged residues. The known DDR-binding epitopes in Col1-Col3 also contain charged residues positioned to interact with those on the DDRs. We hypothesize that these interfacial electrostatic interactions between the DDRs and collagens guide their recognition specificity. We experimentally test this hypothesis and show that triple-helical peptides (THPs) containing rationally placed charged residues have biased affinities for the two DDRs. Aside from advancing mechanistic understanding of the different collagen-DDR interactions, our results can facilitate better understanding of the associated signalling pathways and the design of therapeutically active DDR-specific antagonists.

title: Computational redesign of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii photosynthetic fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase from the Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle improves both stability and catalytic capacities in vitro
abstract: Photosynthetic carbon fixation is catalyzed by 11 enzymes in the Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle, a highly conserved metabolic pathway in the green lineage. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (FBPase) contributes to the regeneration of the substrate of carboxylation. While non-photosynthetic paralogs of FBPases contribute to cytosolic neoglucogenesis in a well-documented manner, chloroplast FBPases specific regulations by phospho- and redox-posttranslational modifications, pH, cofactor binding, and homo-oligomeric exchange is only partially understood. In particular, FBPases from green microalgae are potentially target of a multiplicity of disulfide/dithiol exchanges that appear more complex than all their cytosolic and chloroplastic land-plant or cyanobacterial paralogs. In an attempt to decipher the molecular basis of chloroplast FBPase activities and precise redox regulations, we applied computational tools to extensively redesign its protein coding sequence, testing the simultaneous substitution of >13% of its amino acids as guided by distant homology. Resulting modified proteins in pure recombinant form were significantly more stable than the wild-type starting point, that was prone to denaturation or aggregation. In particular, redesigned FBPase favored the catalytically competent homo-tetrameric state. Thermal denaturation assays revealed that the redesign of FBPase sequence starkly increased in thermostability, in good correlation with an augmented enzymatic activity over long periods of time. By comparison with its wild-type counterpart, computationally redesigned FBPase allowed an extensive structure-function study that uncovered the multiplicity of redox regulations of microalgal paralog, their combined contribution to the assembly of the catalytically competent homo-tetrameric state, and will further facilitate molecular engineering of photosynthesis.

title: Affinity maturation of a single-domain antibody via rational mutagenesis informed by artificial intelligence
abstract: Antibodies can originate from various sources such as animal immunizations, patient material, DNA/RNA libraries and (AI-based) de novo design. Pre-made (e.g. synthetic) DNA libraries have substantial advantages over traditional immunization campaigns in terms of speed, cost, animal welfare, amount of required antigen and the possibility to select against otherwise problematic (e.g. toxic, unstable or expensive) antigens. The main downside is that selections from these non-immune libraries often result in binders with relatively low affinity due to the absence of in vivo affinity maturation. Now that in silico structure prediction tools are coming of age, the resulting models could conceivably be used to rationally design mutations, e.g. to enhance binding affinity. Here we used a synthetic single-domain antibody (sdAb) library to select new binders against interleukin-12 (IL-12). One of the selected candidates, 2F3, was predicted to bind to the p40 subunit of IL-12 in a manner that would compete with binding of the receptor protein IL-12R{beta}1. Intriguingly, this epitope is also targeted by the clinically approved antibodies Briakinumab and Ustekinumab, which are used to treat a variety of inflammation disorders. The predicted structure of the IL-12/sdAb complex was used to rationally design eleven point mutations, of which three showed to enhance the binding affinity. By combining these mutations, we could enhance the affinity by eightfold compared to the original lead clone. This shows that correctly (AI-)predicted protein structural models can be used for rational mutagenesis to enhance binding affinity to relevant drug targets.

title: Molecular arrangements of Thionine within the DNA scaffolds enable machine learning-assisted colorimetric LAMP detection
abstract: In the present work, we describe the distinctive molecular arrangement behavior of the phenothiazine dye - thionine (Th) - in the presence of LAMP amplicons and demonstrate its potential use as a visual indicator for LAMP-based detection. To better understand the mechanism responsible for DNA-templated stacking of Th molecules, detailed photophysical investigations were carried out in the presence of DNA and poly(acrylic acid) (PAA).

title: Density and excess molar enthalpy of 2-butanol + glyme liquid mixtures. Application of the DISQUAC, UNIFAC (Dortmund) and ERAS models to 2-alkanol + linear ether systems
abstract: Densities and excess molar volumes ($V_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$) at (293.15 to 303.15) K and excess molar enthalpies ($H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$) at 298.15 K are reported for the 2-butanol + 2,5-dioxahexane, or + 2,5,8-trioxanonane, or + 2,5,8,11-tetraoxadodecane, or + 2,5,8,11,14-pentaoxapentadecane systems at 95 kPa. Densities were measured using a densitometer Anton Paar DSA 5000, and excess enthalpies by means of a micro-calorimeter Tian-Calvet. $H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ and $V_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ data are positive, indicating that interactions between like molecules are dominant and that the main contribution to $V_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ is the interactional one. Our enthalpic data together with data from the literature have been used to evaluate the enthalpy of alcohol-glyme interactions, which are ranged between ($-$31 and $-$22) kJ mol$^{-1}$. From the comparison with $H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ results for glyme + heptane systems, and from the position of the investigated mixtures in the diagram $G_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ (excess molar Gibbs energy) vs. $H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$, it is shown that interactions are of dispersive type. 2-Alkanol + dipropyl ether (DPE), or + glyme systems have also been studied using the DISQUAC, UNIFAC (Dortmund) and ERAS models. According to ERAS results, physical interactions in glyme systems are dominant, while association effects are predominant in mixtures with DPE. The DISQUAC interaction parameters suggest that interactions related to the OH/O contacts are essentially dispersive. UNIFAC fails when representing thermodynamic properties of the studied solutions.

title: Continual Learning for Reliable In-Sequence Molecular Communication
abstract: This paper considers reliable in-sequence molecular communication, where bio-nanomachines exchange molecule-encoded information in a specified order, and investigates a new simulation-based method to incrementally evaluate communication protocols by gradually increasing the complexity of experimental settings. The proposed method, called Affine Memory Replay (AMR), builds a continual learning (CL) model to estimate communication performance between bio-nanomachines. AMR stores past simulation samples and synthesizes additional replay samples through interpolation and extrapolation between past samples. Through incremental performance estimation tasks, it replays both past and synthetic samples to regularize model updates, helping the model adapt to new experimental settings while retaining knowledge from earlier ones. Experimental results show that AMR significantly outperforms existing CL methods in maintaining overall estimation accuracy across sequentially learned estimation tasks. It effectively balances memory stability and learning plasticity under moderate training cost.

title: EvolvingBrain: An Adaptive Skill System for Multi-modal Agents Self-Evolution in Open Worlds
abstract: Multi-modal agents have made significant progress in interacting with open worlds. However, their ability to self-evolve remains limited. Supervised fine-tuning enables imitation but not active experience organization, while outcome-based reinforcement learning promotes exploration yet underuses intermediate trajectory information. Therefore, we propose EvolvingBrain, which uses an adaptive skill system as the brain for agent self-evolution, consisting of two following components. Stratified Skill Self-Evolution: extracts Procedural Patterns and Problematic Patterns from model-specific trajectories, summarizes experience by generating skills, and evolves through multiple interactions with the open world, ultimately forming a Stratified Skill Architecture consisting of Domain, Plan, and Action/Trap Skills, which provides the agent with a multi-granularity knowledge repository and a novel evolution approach. State-Aware Adaptive Execution: summarizes long-horizon interactions into Structured Abstractive Memory and uses it to guide the State-Aware Skill Fusion Strategy, enabling the agent to utilize knowledge according to its current state. Experiments on VAB-Minecraft and DiscoveryWorld demonstrate that EvolvingBrain improves success rates on open-world tasks and exhibits generalization capabilities. Our code is provided in the supplementary materials and will be publicly released in the camera-ready version.

title: A constructive solution to the $n$-representability problem
abstract: We present an instantiation of the constructive solution to the fermionic quantum marginal problem by building the complete family of two-body witnesses at each level of a weighted sum-of-squares hierarchy. Our construction combines positive-semidefinite Gram matrices with explicit linear nullspace constraints that exactly cancel all higher-body contributions following a similar idea to the existing solution but made explicit in open source software.
